definition: In machine learning, mode collapse is a failure mode observed in generative models, originally noted in Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs).
details: It occurs when the model produces outputs that are less diverse than expected, effectively "collapsing" to generate only a few modes of the data distribution while ignoring others. This phenomenon undermines the goal of generative models to capture the full diversity of the training data. There are typically two times at which a model can collapse: either during training or during post-training finetuning. Mode collapse reduces the utility of generative models in applications, such as in image synthesis (repetitive or near-identical images); data augmentation (limited diversity in synthetic data); scientific simulations (failure to explore all plausible scenarios).

explainer.lead: Mode collapse is a failure mode in generative models, originally noted in GANs, where outputs are less diverse than expected. It undermines the goal of capturing the full diversity of the training data.

tiers.eli5: It's when a generator gets stuck producing the same few things over and over instead of the variety it was supposed to learn.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers watch output diversity during training and finetuning to catch collapse early. The pitfall is that a model can look good on individual samples while silently ignoring whole regions of the data distribution.
tiers.paperLevel: A generative model collapses to a few modes of the data distribution while ignoring others, producing outputs less diverse than expected. Collapse can occur either during training or during post-training finetuning.

explainer.example: A generative model trained on images of many animals might only ever produce cats and dogs, never the other species present in the data.
